title: Orthopaedic rehabilitation: rapid review of wearable activity feedback after knee replacement before a device lease decision
notes: Routine path with clean inputs: the need names a rapid review, so routing is explicit at create. A fixture search returns seven well-formed records with abstracts (years 2016 to 2024); the appraisal call annotates all seven by id and records five source-derived claims whose passages are exact substrings of the abstracts; certainty "low" is the appraisal's own value over inspected records. The problem reply restates the investigator's constraints verbatim, so G11 leaves them unchanged with no issue. A reload between the Design stage and the acceptance checks that a proposed decision survives a reload. The decision rests on ledger claims c1, c2 and c4 and both gates are met on investigator-supplied records, so acceptance gives selectionStatus accepted and actionStatus ready. Record ids are not typed by hand: each is stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts, computed by the generator script: 'ev-' plus the base-36 FNV-1a hash of the normalised DOI (records 1, 2, 4, 6, 7: ev-14bc9ym, ev-1gkku0k, ev-0f90usc, ev-0bvjgav, ev-1hrnbpa) or of titleYearKey(title, year) when there is no DOI (records 3, 5: ev-1f7dnlu, ev-1udqr2q). Requires S13 (appraisal dispatched on the production scan path), S11 (routing basis at create, selectionStatus, actionStatus, basis 'explicit' on acceptance) and D5 (decision status text on screen). Catches: certainty or completion without retrieval, claims that never reach the ledger, a proposed decision lost on reload, acceptance without ledger support, and an export that differs from the store.

inputs.need:
I lead the outpatient physiotherapy service at a regional orthopaedic centre that does a little over 900 primary total knee replacements a year. Our rehabilitation after discharge is six weeks of group and home exercise, with a physiotherapy review at two, six and twelve weeks. A supplier has offered us a 12-month lease of 150 wrist-worn activity trackers with an app that sets daily step targets and lets a physiotherapist see each patient's step counts on a dashboard and send short messages of encouragement or advice. The procurement committee will decide on 10 December 2026 whether to fund it, and the chair has asked for an evidence summary first.

What I need is a rapid review, done properly but within eight weeks, of what wearable-based activity feedback does after knee replacement: does it improve physical function and activity at around three months compared with usual rehabilitation, how many patients actually keep wearing the device, and what it costs in physiotherapist time to look at the data. I also want to know whether older patients, people without a smartphone and people living alone benefit less, because about a third of our patients are over 75 and many live in rural areas with poor mobile coverage.

I have an information specialist from the library for 20 hours and two physiotherapists who can each give a day a week. We cannot translate papers, and I do not want a summary that simply repeats the supplier's brochure. The output should be a short report that tells the committee what the evidence shows, how certain it is, and what a local evaluation would need to answer if we go ahead.
inputs.constraints: Report due to the procurement committee on 10 December 2026, eight weeks after protocol sign-off. Searching is limited to 20 hours of information specialist time; two physiotherapists at one day a week each do screening and extraction. English-language sources only.
localFacts: The library service confirmed 20 hours of information specialist time between 5 October and 27 November 2026 (request LIB-2026-311).
The procurement committee has listed the wearable lease decision for its meeting of 10 December 2026 (agenda item PC-26-44).
The centre performed 912 primary total knee replacements in the 2025-26 financial year; 34 percent of patients were aged 75 or over.

steps.query: wearable activity tracker feedback after total knee replacement function step count adherence

records.title: Wearable activity trackers with feedback after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.authors: Halvorsen-Mbeki T, Carrow-Adeyemi J, Lindqvist-Oduya P
records.abstract: We searched five bibliographic databases from inception to March 2022 for randomised trials comparing activity tracker feedback with usual rehabilitation after primary total knee arthroplasty. Eleven trials with 1,146 participants met the criteria. Feedback increased daily step count at 12 weeks (mean difference 1,090 steps, 95 percent CI 540 to 1,640; eight trials) but did not clearly improve patient-reported function (standardised mean difference 0.12, 95 percent CI -0.05 to 0.29; nine trials). Heterogeneity was high for steps. Most trials were at some risk of bias from unblinded outcome assessment, and none reported results separately for patients over 75. Certainty was moderate for steps and low for function.

records.title: Remote step-count feedback versus usual physiotherapy after knee replacement: a multicentre trial
records.authors: Castell-Nwosu R, Brightman-Oyelaran K, Tanaka-Ferris D, Obi-Lundgren S
records.abstract: Two hundred and twelve adults were randomly allocated after primary knee replacement to a wrist-worn tracker with weekly physiotherapist feedback on step targets or to usual physiotherapy. At 12 weeks the feedback group walked more (median 5,900 versus 4,700 steps per day), but the difference in patient-reported knee function was small and uncertain (2.1 points on a 48-point scale, 95 percent CI -0.8 to 5.0). Device wear on at least five days a week fell from 78 percent at week 6 to 61 percent at week 12. There were no differences in falls or readmissions. Physiotherapists spent a median of 4 minutes per patient per week on feedback.

records.title: Who stops wearing it? Adherence to activity trackers among older adults after joint replacement
records.abstract: We followed 318 adults aged 65 and over who were given an activity tracker after hip or knee replacement and recorded whether data were synchronised each week for 12 weeks. Twenty-three percent never synchronised any data. Stopping within four weeks was more common in people aged over 80, people without a smartphone and people living alone. Patients who stopped reported difficulty charging the device, skin irritation and a sense that nobody looked at the data. The study could not tell whether stopping affected recovery, because function was not measured after discharge from the programme.

records.title: Physiotherapist time spent reviewing remote activity data: a time-and-motion study in three orthopaedic services
records.authors: Olumide-Sandberg E, Rourke-Achterberg N, Vasquez-Holm T
records.abstract: Fourteen physiotherapists in three orthopaedic services recorded the time they spent on dashboards of patients' activity data after joint replacement over eight weeks. Reviewing the data and messaging patients took a median of 3.5 minutes per patient per week (interquartile range 2.0 to 6.0), with most time spent on patients whose step counts fell. Threshold alerts produced many prompts that led to no action, and two services switched them off. Physiotherapists valued the data for patients who lived far from the clinic but felt that reviews displaced face-to-face time when caseloads were high.

records.title: Early walking volume and function six months after total knee replacement: a secondary analysis of exercise study data
records.abstract: Using step counts recorded in the sixth week after surgery by 406 participants of an exercise study, we examined whether walking volume predicted patient-reported function at six months. Each additional 1,000 steps per day was associated with a 1.4-point better function score, but the association fell to 0.5 points (95 percent CI -0.2 to 1.2) after adjustment for pre-operative function and pain. Walking volume may mark recovery rather than cause it, so raising step counts alone may not improve function. Participants were younger and fitter than typical surgical patients.

records.title: Rapid reviews for hospital technology decisions: agreement with full systematic reviews on the direction of effect
records.authors: Whitcombe-Eze L, Sorensen-Baptiste H, Quayle-Moreno R
records.abstract: We compared 30 rapid reviews produced for hospital technology decisions with full systematic reviews on the same questions. Conclusions agreed on the direction of effect in 27 of 30 pairs. Rapid reviews more often missed non-English and grey literature and less often reported a risk of bias assessment. Disagreements arose where the evidence base was small or changing quickly. We recommend that rapid reviews state every shortcut taken, date their searches and say which conclusions would change if a missed study pointed the other way.

records.title: Being watched or being supported? Patients' experience of app-based activity feedback in knee rehabilitation
records.abstract: We interviewed 22 patients who had used an activity tracker with physiotherapist feedback for 12 weeks after knee replacement. Most valued seeing their progress and said that messages from a named physiotherapist kept them walking. Several felt judged by daily step targets on days when pain or swelling limited walking, and some stopped wearing the device after a week of low counts. Patients in areas with poor mobile coverage described missed synchronisation and repeated reminders. Participants asked for targets that could be adjusted and for someone to explain what the data were used for.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Feedback from wearable trackers raises daily steps after knee replacement (about 1,090 steps at 12 weeks across eight trials) but a clear gain in patient-reported function has not been shown, and walking volume may mark recovery rather than cause it. Device wear falls from about four in five patients at six weeks to three in five at twelve, and stopping is more common in the oldest patients, people without smartphones and people living alone, who are a large share of this centre's patients. Physiotherapist review takes a few minutes per patient per week. The retrieved meta-analysis searched only to March 2022, so a dated rapid update focused on function, adherence, workload and older patients is justified.
response.gradeRationale: Moderate certainty that feedback increases steps, but low certainty about function, the outcome that matters most for the decision: unblinded outcomes, imprecision around a small effect, and indirectness for patients over 75. Adherence and workload evidence comes from single observational studies.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty low because function is uncertain.

Device wear falls over 12 weeks (claim c3) and stopping is more common among the oldest patients, people without smartphones and people living alone (claim c4), a large share of this centre's patients. Physiotherapist review time is small per patient but adds up across a caseload (claim c5).

response.rationale: The committee needs an answer by 10 December 2026 and the service has eight weeks, 20 information specialist hours and two part-time reviewers. A rapid review with stated shortcuts (a dated update search from January 2022, single screening with a 20 percent check, English only) can update the existing meta-analysis for function at about three months (claims c1, c2) and summarise adherence (c3), older and digitally excluded patients (c4) and physiotherapist time (c5). Rapid and full reviews usually agree on the direction of effect when shortcuts are reported.

response.overview: Rapid review with documented shortcuts, updating the 2023 meta-analysis for patient-reported function at about three months and summarising adherence, physiotherapist time, patient experience and results for older and digitally excluded patients, reported to the procurement committee on 10 December 2026.
response.population: Adults after primary total knee replacement in randomised trials (effectiveness) and in qualitative or observational studies (adherence, workload, experience) published from January 2015 in English.
response.exposure: Wearable-based activity feedback in the first 12 weeks after surgery: a worn device that records activity with feedback to the patient through targets, app messages or physiotherapist messages. Comparator: usual rehabilitation or the same device without feedback.
response.procedures: The information specialist searches three bibliographic databases and two trial registries from January 2022 to October 2026 with a dated strategy and checks the reference list of the 2023 meta-analysis. One physiotherapist screens titles and abstracts and the second checks a random 20 percent; full texts are screened by one reviewer and disagreements discussed. One reviewer extracts data into a tested form and the second checks every primary outcome value. Trials are judged with a short domain-based risk of bias tool; qualitative studies are summarised thematically. Function is pooled if at least five trials report it; otherwise effect directions are tabulated.

outcomes.why: Low adherence limits benefit and raises the cost per active user.

outcomes.why: Clinic time is the main hidden cost of the lease.

outcomes.why: More walking in the early weeks could bring more falls.

response.designSummary: Rapid review with an updated random-effects meta-analysis for the primary outcome when at least five trials report it.
response.sampleSize: The unit of analysis is the trial. The 2023 meta-analysis pooled nine trials for function; if the update adds two or three trials, a random-effects meta-analysis of about 11 trials and 1,200 participants gives a 95 percent confidence interval roughly 0.12 either side of the standardised mean difference, enough to separate a patient-important effect (0.3 or more) from little or no effect (below 0.2). With fewer than five trials reporting function the review will not pool.
response.primaryAnalysis: Random-effects meta-analysis (restricted maximum likelihood with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment) of standardised mean differences in function at about three months; certainty rated with GRADE.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Mean difference in daily steps; adherence and physiotherapist time summarised as medians and ranges across studies; qualitative findings grouped into themes; results for patients aged 75 or over extracted where reported.
response.missingData: No author contact in the time available; trials reporting only medians are included with a standard conversion and removed in a sensitivity analysis.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary outcomes described with intervals and no significance testing.

Supplier-funded trials removed in one sensitivity analysis only

response.title: Wearable activity feedback after total knee replacement: a rapid review to inform a device lease decision
response.abstract: Objective: to update the evidence on whether wearable-based activity feedback after primary total knee replacement improves patient-reported function at about three months, and to summarise adherence, physiotherapist time and results for older and digitally excluded patients. Design: rapid review with a dated update search from January 2022, single screening with a 20 percent check and stated shortcuts. Results and conclusions will be written after the synthesis.
response.introduction: Activity trackers with feedback raise step counts after knee replacement, but whether they improve function is uncertain and the most recent synthesis searched to March 2022. A regional centre must decide whether to lease devices for about 900 patients a year, a third of them aged 75 or over.
response.methods: Three bibliographic databases and two trial registries were searched from January 2022 to October 2026 and the 2023 meta-analysis was used as the base. Randomised trials informed effectiveness; qualitative and observational studies informed adherence, workload and experience. Function at about three months was pooled with a random-effects model when at least five trials reported it.
response.results: No studies have been screened yet. The report will present the search flow, the updated pooled estimate for function with its certainty, step counts, adherence at 6 and 12 weeks, physiotherapist time and results for older patients where reported.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh a probable step count gain against the size and certainty of any function gain, set adherence and workload against the lease cost, and state what a local evaluation would need to measure if the committee proceeds.
response.limitations: Shortcuts may miss studies; English only; no author contact; few trials report results for patients over 75.
response.conclusion: To be written after the synthesis; it will be limited to what the evidence shows about function, adherence and workload and will not claim benefits for groups the trials did not include.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I lead the outpatient physiotherapy service at a regional orthopaedic centre that does a little over 900 primary total knee replacements a year. Our rehabilitation after discharge is six weeks of group and home exercise, with a physiotherapy review at two, six and twelve weeks. A supplier has offered us a 12-month lease of 150 wrist-worn activity trackers with an app that sets daily step targets and lets a physiotherapist see each patient's step counts on a dashboard and send short messages of encouragement or advice. The procurement committee will decide on 10 December 2026 whether to fund it, and the chair has asked for an evidence summary first.

What I need is a rapid review, done properly but within eight weeks, of what wearable-based activity feedback does after knee replacement: does it improve physical function and activity at around three months compared with usual rehabilitation, how many patients actually keep wearing the device, and what it costs in physiotherapist time to look at the data. I also want to know whether older patients, people without a smartphone and people living alone benefit less, because about a third of our patients are over 75 and many live in rural areas with poor mobile coverage.

I have an information specialist from the library for 20 hours and two physiotherapists who can each give a day a week. We cannot translate papers, and I do not want a summary that simply repeats the supplier's brochure. The output should be a short report that tells the committee what the evidence shows, how certain it is, and what a local evaluation would need to answer if we go ahead.
